extracted.intended_audience: general public and historians studying Lincoln's speeches (citizens of 1861 and later readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of short public replies and addresses delivered by Abraham Lincoln during his February 1861 tour on the way to his inauguration; focuses on greetings, reassurance, restraint from policy detail, and appeals to unity. Useful for studying presidential rhetoric, protocol for receptions, and public reassurance in a national crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearances for visibility not speech
rubrics_metrics.description: "I appear before you that I may see you, and that you may see me;" (I have no speech to make to you; and no time to speak in.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many addresses state explicitly that the purpose is to greet and be seen rather than to deliver an extended address. Use brief remarks when the occasion is primarily ceremonial or when repeated stops make long speeches impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept receptions as representative of institutions, not personal honor
rubrics_metrics.description: "This reception... is not given to me personally,--it should not be so,--but as the representative, for the time being, of the majority of the nation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When receiving public honors, frame gratitude as recognition of the office or the nation's institutions rather than personal aggrandizement; consistently deflect personal credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer policy specifics until official/appropriate time
rubrics_metrics.description: "I do not propose to enter into an explanation of any particular line of policy... for this reason I do not propose to speak at this time of the policy of the Government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid detailing policy positions in informal or preliminary appearances; indicate intention to speak officially at a set time after consultation and information-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize preservation of Union, Constitution, and liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated affirmations that receptions manifest devotion "to the Constitution, the Union, and to the perpetual liberties of succeeding generations" and that efforts aim to "preserve the Union."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center public rhetoric on shared constitutional principles and the nation's continuity; portray actions as in service of enduring institutions and liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humble and modest tone
rubrics_metrics.description: "I hold myself... the humblest of all individuals that have ever been elevated to the Presidency" and "I appropriate to myself very little of the demonstrations of respect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt modest language, downplay personal importance, and attribute success or ceremony to the people or providence rather than to the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage patience and restraint among the public
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we have patience, if we restrain ourselves, if we allow ourselves not to run off in a passion, I still have confidence..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calming appeals to patience and temper public passions as a rhetorical strategy during crises; advocate waiting for measured, informed action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise peaceful intent but assert readiness to act in self-defence
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am not in favor of such a course [bloodshed]... there will be no bloodshed unless it is forced upon the Government... it may be necessary to put the foot down firmly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reassure audiences of a preference for peace while also making clear that the government will act decisively if compelled; balance conciliation with resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal across party and sectional lines; seek broad support
rubrics_metrics.description: "This reception... doubtless emanates from all the political parties..." and accepting receptions "without distinction of party."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame appeals inclusively, acknowledge political differences, and emphasize shared commitments to national goals to solicit cooperation from diverse constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with thanks and keep remarks brief when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent openings: "I thank you very kindly for this great reception"; many remarks end with brief thanks and farewells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with gratitude; when time or strength is limited, offer concise remarks rather than lengthy addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speaking when unprepared or physically unable
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have neither strength nor time to address you at any greater length... I have not sufficient time, if I had the strength, to repeat speeches at every station... I have no speech to make."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer silence or brief greetings over ill-prepared or exhaustive speaking when fatigued or pressed for time; acknowledge limitations candidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground political sentiment in founding documents
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the political sentiments I entertain have been drawn... from the sentiments which originated and were given to the world from this hall... the Declaration of Independence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor public arguments in widely respected national founding texts to lend legitimacy and common reference points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassure constituencies with different institutions of equal respect
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have not now, and never have had, any disposition to treat you... otherwise than as my own neighbors... I have not now any purpose to withhold from you any of the benefits of the Constitution..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing populations with differing institutions or concerns, explicitly assure them of equal treatment under the Constitution and respect from the speaker's section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute success to the people and providence rather than oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: "I had not provided the flag; I had not made the arrangements... I was in the hands of the people... I was a very humbled instrument."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deflect credit to organizers, citizens, or divine agency to cultivate humility and shared ownership of public ceremonies and achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep public statements general to avoid misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more a man speaks the less he is understood--the more he says one thing, the more his adversaries contend he meant something else."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise, general statements over detailed, technical language in public appearances to reduce opportunities for opponents to misconstrue or over-interpret remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult widely and gather information before taking a public stance
rubrics_metrics.description: "I should see everything, that I should hear everything, that I should have every light that can be brought within my reach..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate an intention to listen to diverse inputs and delay definitive public positions until adequately informed; present deliberation as a virtue.
